newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - Eyes firmly on India.
newsitem.headline: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - Eyes firmly on India.

text.p: Gulf oil product traders are turning to India Oil Corp's (IOC) December gas oil buying tender as the clearest guide to short-term market direction in the region, traders said on Thursday.

With outright Gulf prices and premiums stuck in a sideways pattern near five-year highs and Iraq's on-off oil deal again off the boil, traders are waiting to see how much IOC will take from an already tight market to fuel its upcoming harvest.
"The biggest determinant in the middle of the barrel is how much they (IOC) will take in the tender," a trader said.
Bids for IOC's tender must be received by today and be valid for two days.
December traditionally sees heavy IOC buying.
IOC sparked a surge in middle distillate markets last year when it first bought 15 cargoes of gas oil, some 530,000 tonnes, in its December tender before issuing a supplementary tender.
But this year's purchasing level has been complicated by severe port congestion at the Kandla terminal on the Indian west coast which could blunt IOC's import capacity.
Congestion at Kandla was made worse this week after two diesel tankers collided, knocking out one operational jetty.

"The market is intrigued whether the problems at Kandla will keep IOC away from the market or that their harvest need and scant purchases over the last three months will drive them to buy more or pay high demurrage costs," a Gulf trader said.
Traders have been disappointed by recent IOC imports which have effectively kept a cap on strong spot premiums.
Gas oil was assessed at around $28.40 a barrel fob Gulf on Thursday with premiums between 90 cents and $1.00.
Traders said that gas oil was now commanding a slight outright price premium against jet.
Middle distillate fundamentals contrasted with gas oil cargoes in tight supply while jet cargoes struggled to find homes in Asia because of higher South Korea and Thai exports.
Jet's premium to quotes was assessed at 40 to 50 cents.
Gulf naphtha and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) prices are expected to remain in sight of post Gulf War highs because of strong Asian petrochemical and heating demand and limited cargo supplies.
In term product negotiations, Saudi Aramco is continuing talks in London with major product lifters for 1997 supplies.
Traders said they expected Aramco to wrap up at least part of its term supplies by early next week.
